werk/robert-glasper-double-booked.text:
Double Booked is the fourth studio album by the American pianist and producer Robert Glasper and was released on 25 August 2009 on Blue Note Records. It was recorded in New York, at Systems 2 Studios and Brooklyn Recording. He produced the album entirely himself. The two halves have different line-ups. On the first six tracks Vicente Archer plays double bass; on the last six, Derrick Hodge on bass guitar and Casey Benjamin on alto saxophone and vocoder can be heard. Drummer Chris Dave plays throughout.

The album also features guests. Terence Blanchard lends his voice, Mos Def raps and Questlove chimes in on one track. Bilal sings on the last two pieces, and Jahi Sundance spins scratches on the closing track.
werk/robert-glasper-double-booked.listen: Listen to the beginning and the end of the album and notice how the line-up changes, from double bass to bass guitar, vocoder and scratches.

werk/robert-glasper-in-my-element.text:
In My Element is the third studio album by pianist Robert Glasper and was released on 20 March 2007 on Blue Note. It was recorded at Systems Two Studios in Brooklyn, between 21 September and 1 November 2006. He produced it himself together with Eli Wolf and plays in a trio with bassist Vicente Archer and drummer Damion Reid.

On one of the tracks the spoken voice of Reverend Joe Ratliff can be heard. The track list also includes a piece that combines Maiden Voyage and Everything In Its Right Place in a single title, and a piece for the pianist Mulgrew Miller. In the United States the album reached number 9 on the Jazz Albums chart and number 6 on the Traditional Jazz Albums chart.
werk/robert-glasper-in-my-element.listen: In Maiden Voyage / Everything In Its Right Place, see whether you can hear both titles in the music.

werk/robert-plant-now-and-zen.text:
Now and Zen was released on 29 February 1988 on Es Paranza Records, Robert Plant's own label. It is his fourth solo album, produced by Tim Palmer, Plant himself and Phil Johnstone. Jimmy Page, the guitarist of Led Zeppelin, plays the guitar solos on Heaven Knows and Tall Cool One. On the latter, Plant also used samples of Led Zeppelin, as a response to the Beastie Boys, who on their 1986 album had sampled pieces of that band without permission.

The record reached number 6 in the United States and number 10 in the United Kingdom. Reviewers responded positively. Kurt Loder wrote in Rolling Stone of a seamless pop fusion of hard guitar rock and computer sound. He later felt that many songs had been lost in the technology of the time.
werk/robert-plant-now-and-zen.listen: Listen to Tall Cool One and try to recognise the Led Zeppelin samples. Also notice Jimmy Page's guitar solo.

werk/robert-plant-pictures-at-eleven.text:
After Led Zeppelin, Robert Plant embarked on a solo career. Pictures at Eleven was released in the summer of 1982 and is his first solo album. It came out on Swan Song, the label of his old band, and is the only solo album released there. The title comes from American television news, where a story would be trailed in this way for the eleven o'clock news. Phil Collins of Genesis played drums on five of the eight tracks, Cozy Powell on Slow Dancer and Like I've Never Been Gone. On Fat Lip, guitarist Robbie Blunt operated a drum machine, the Roland TR-808.

Critics heard mainly an echo of Led Zeppelin. Kurt Loder wrote in Rolling Stone that nothing new was happening, but found the craftsmanship almost an event. The Boston Phoenix saw the album largely as a derivative of Led Zeppelin. Robert Christgau admired how the singer evoked that sound with lesser musicians, but ultimately found the music unimportant.
werk/robert-plant-pictures-at-eleven.listen: Listen to Fat Lip and notice the rhythm: it does not come from a drummer, but from a drum machine operated by the guitarist.

werk/robert-plant-shaken-n-stirred.text:
Shaken 'n' Stirred is Robert Plant's third solo album. It was released on 20 May 1985 on his own label Es Paranza Records. He produced it together with Benji Le Fevre and Tim Palmer. He later said that he was greatly impressed by Talking Heads and therefore kept writing ever more unusual music, using new studio techniques. At times, he said himself, this made him lose his way.

The single Little by Little spent two weeks at the top of the Mainstream Rock chart, and Sixes and Sevens also became a hit there. According to Plant, Too Loud is a funny song that was misunderstood. For the backing vocals he asked singers from Bette Midler's entourage. In 2007 a remastered edition appeared with an additional track.
werk/robert-plant-shaken-n-stirred.listen: Listen to Too Loud and notice the backing vocals and the playful tone. Can you hear the influence of Talking Heads?

werk/robert-plant-the-principle-of-momen.text:
With The Principle of Moments, Robert Plant released his second solo album in 1983, after Pictures at Eleven. Swan Song no longer existed, so he started a label of his own, Es Paranza, which was distributed through Atlantic. Phil Collins again played drums on five of the eight tracks, Barriemore Barlow, formerly of Jethro Tull, on two. On the closing track Big Log, Gerald Woodroffe programmed a drum machine, the Roland TR-808.

Like its predecessor, the sound departed from the hard rock of Led Zeppelin. Other Arms was the most popular song on American album rock radio and reached number one on the Billboard Top Tracks. Big Log became his first solo hit in the American top 40. The album reached the American and British top 10. A tour followed in 1983, on which Collins was the band's drummer in North America.
werk/robert-plant-the-principle-of-momen.listen: Listen to Big Log, the closing track, and notice the rhythm: it comes from a programmed drum machine instead of a drummer.

werk/rod-stewart-an-old-raincoat-won-t-e.text:
An Old Raincoat Won't Ever Let You Down is Rod Stewart's solo debut. In the United States it was released in November 1969 under the title The Rod Stewart Album; in the United Kingdom the revised title followed in February 1970. His later Faces colleagues Ronnie Wood and Ian McLagan play on it, alongside, among others, Keith Emerson, drummer Micky Waller and guitarists Martin Pugh and Martin Quittenton.

The album combines versions of other people's work, such as Street Fighting Man, Man of Constant Sorrow and Dirty Old Town, with original pieces. On Handbags & Gladrags, Mike d'Abo plays piano. Fusion, Rolling Stone and Robert Christgau were positive. Rolling Stone saw Stewart as a highly individual interpreter of other people's songs who could be disarmingly vulnerable in his own work.
werk/rod-stewart-an-old-raincoat-won-t-e.listen: In Man of Constant Sorrow, listen to the voice and the guitar, and notice how Stewart bends a familiar song to his will.

werk/rod-stewart-every-picture-tells-a-s.text:
In 1971 Rod Stewart was also the singer of the Faces, and all five band members contribute to his third studio album, which was released in May 1971 on Mercury Records. Ronnie Wood on guitar and bass and Ian McLagan on Hammond organ in particular can be heard a great deal. Others playing include Ray Jackson on mandolin, Martin Quittenton on acoustic guitar and Pete Sears on piano.

The album mixes rock, country, blues, soul and folk. Reason to Believe, a song by Tim Hardin, was intended as the first single, but the B-side Maggie May became the big hit and reached number one in England and America. There is also a version of That's All Right (Mama), Elvis Presley's first single, and a cover of Bob Dylan. The album itself spent six weeks at the top in England and four in America. Critics still praise it, and Mandolin Wind is regarded as the best original song.
werk/rod-stewart-every-picture-tells-a-s.listen: In Mandolin Wind, listen to the mandolin, which gives the song its folk colour.

werk/rod-stewart-gasoline-alley.text:
Gasoline Alley is Rod Stewart's second solo album and was released on 12 June 1970 on Vertigo Records. It contains covers alongside original compositions. As on many of his solo records of the period, the other members of the Faces make a substantial contribution, including Ronnie Wood, Ronnie Lane, Ian McLagan and Kenney Jones. Stewart produced the record together with Lou Reizner.

The title track later enjoyed a second life: Elkie Brooks had a hit with it in 1983, and Long John Baldry, with whom Stewart had played earlier, recorded it in 1973. The reception was good. Langdon Winner of Rolling Stone felt that Stewart had a feeling for the fragile moments in a human life and called it the work of an exceptionally fine artist.
werk/rod-stewart-gasoline-alley.listen: In Country Comfort, listen to the piano and the backing vocals and notice the relaxed mood of the song.

werk/rod-stewart-smiler.text:
Smiler is Rod Stewart's fifth solo album and was released on 27 September 1974. It came out on Mercury Records, after a five-month delay caused by legal problems between Mercury and Warner Bros. The album reached number 1 on the British album chart and number 13 on the American.

Members of the Faces and regular collaborators such as Martin Quittenton, Pete Sears and Mickey Waller play on the record. It contains covers of Chuck Berry, Sam Cooke and Bob Dylan. There is also a duet with Elton John on John's song Let Me Be Your Car, and a version of Carole King's (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Man, in which Woman has been changed to Man. The single Farewell, which he wrote together with Quittenton, reached the British top ten. In the United States the B-side Mine for Me, written by Paul and Linda McCartney, became a minor hit.
werk/rod-stewart-smiler.listen: Listen to Let Me Be Your Car and notice the two voices: this is a duet with Elton John, the writer of the song.

werk/rodgers-en-hammerstein-oklahoma.text: On 31 March 1943 the musical Oklahoma! opened at the St. James Theatre in New York, the first work by composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist Oscar Hammerstein. The songs carry the story forward, rather than standing apart from it. The show ran for well over two thousand performances. At the end of 1943 Decca released the songs, sung by the original cast: the first major cast album. Broadway became a supplier of hits.
werk/rodgers-en-hammerstein-oklahoma.listen: Hear how the show begins with a single lone voice singing about a beautiful morning, with no great spectacle.

werk/roger-daltrey-daltrey.text:
Daltrey is the first solo album by Roger Daltrey, singer of The Who. It was released on 20 April 1973 on Track Records in the United Kingdom and on MCA in the United States. Recording took six weeks, in January and February 1973, during a break in the band's touring schedule. The backing tracks were made in his own Barn Studio in Burwash, the rest at the Beatles' Apple Studios and at Nova Sound Studios. Ten of the twelve songs were written by David Courtney and Leo Sayer.

Courtney and Sayer supplied the songs after he had jokingly asked Sayer for material. The opening track One Man Band later became one of Sayer's own biggest hits. The single Giving It All Away reached number five in Britain and the album entered the American top 50. The press was divided: Robert Christgau called it yet another silly concept record, while AllMusic later spoke of a pleasant surprise.
werk/roger-daltrey-daltrey.listen: Listen to Giving It All Away and notice how the singer takes the lead here, apart from his bandmates.

werk/roger-daltrey-ride-a-rock-horse.text:
Ride a Rock Horse is the second solo album by the English singer Roger Daltrey. It was released on 4 July 1975 on Track in the United Kingdom and on MCA in the United States. The record was made while he was also busy filming Lisztomania, a film by Ken Russell. On the cover, designed and photographed by his cousin Graham Hughes, he appears as an exuberant centaur.

Three singles were released: Get Your Love, Walking the Dog and Oceans Away. Walking the Dog is a version of a song by Rufus Thomas and reached number 52 on the British chart. The album itself reached number 14 in Britain and number 28 in the United States. For Hearts Right, Gerald Scarfe made a video with drawings and animation. Scarfe later became known for his work for Pink Floyd.
werk/roger-daltrey-ride-a-rock-horse.listen: Listen to Walking the Dog and consider how the singer turns this older Rufus Thomas song into a version of his own.

werk/ron-carter-blues-farm.text:
Blues Farm is an album by bassist Ron Carter, recorded on 10 January 1973 at Van Gelder's studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, and released on the label CTI. Carter is not only the bassist but also the arranger and conductor of the session. He works with, among others, flautist Hubert Laws, the pianists Richard Tee and Bob James, drummer Billy Cobham and percussionist Ralph MacDonald.

Of the six pieces, five are by Carter himself. Django is a composition by John Lewis. The pieces run from just under three to well over eight minutes. The AllMusic reviewer found the excursions pleasant, but rather reserved. Both the compositions and the playing avoid strong emotions, he wrote, and opt for pleasant colours and textures.
werk/ron-carter-blues-farm.listen: Listen to Blues Farm and notice how the bass, the flute and the electric piano together create a mood, without any high emotion coming into play.

werk/ron-carter-uptown-conversation.text:
Uptown Conversation is the second album led by bassist Ron Carter, recorded in 1969 and first released on the label Embryo. Carter plays both electric bass and double bass. He has an unusual line-up around him: Hubert Laws on flute, Herbie Hancock on piano and electric piano, Sam Brown on guitar and the drummers Grady Tate and Billy Cobham.

The record contains seven pieces by Carter himself, with two alternate takes as a bonus on the CD reissue. Michael Nastos of AllMusic called it perhaps the most intriguing, challenging and impressive statement Carter has made as a leader. He considered it one of the most varied, intellectually stimulating and free records of his long career.
werk/ron-carter-uptown-conversation.listen: In Uptown Conversation, listen to the interplay of electric bass, flute and piano, as if the instruments were holding a conversation.

werk/ron-carter-where.text:
Where? is the debut album of bassist Ron Carter, recorded in 1961 at Van Gelder Studio and released on the label New Jazz. Some reissues appear under the name of Eric Dolphy, who plays bass clarinet, alto saxophone and flute on it. Besides the bass, Carter also plays the cello. We also hear Mal Waldron, George Duvivier and Charlie Persip.

Carter and Dolphy had already played together in Chico Hamilton's group. According to AllMusic, Where? is closer to Hamilton's chamber jazz than to Dolphy's adventurous 1960 record Out There. The reviewer found Carter's playing somewhat polite and monotonous and Dolphy the more interesting player.
werk/ron-carter-where.listen: In Softly, as in a Morning Sunrise, listen to Eric Dolphy's alto saxophone and notice how he handles the familiar melody.

werk/roscoe-mitchell-hey-donald.text:
Hey Donald was recorded in 1994 and released on the label Delmark. It was the first recording of a quartet with pianist Jodie Christian, bassist Malachi Favors and drummer Albert Tootie Heath, built around saxophonist Roscoe Mitchell. The album is dedicated to Donald Myrick, saxophonist of Earth, Wind and Fire.

The leader plays alto, tenor, soprano and sopranino saxophone and flute. According to AllMusic, he saves the more bop-like pieces for his tenor saxophone, while his soprano, with an intense sound, conjures up a kind of drone, somewhat reminiscent of bagpipes. The album contains twelve tracks, also by the quartet members themselves and by Lester Bowie. The Penguin Guide to Jazz was more mixed: when the rhythm section plays tightly in time and lays down a groove, the honking of the saxophone sometimes sounds downright ridiculous.
werk/roscoe-mitchell-hey-donald.listen: Listen to Hey Donald and notice the difference between the various saxophones and how the rhythm section keeps playing underneath.

werk/roswell-rudd-everywhere.text:
Everywhere was recorded in New York on 8 July 1966 for the label Impulse! Trombonist Roswell Rudd got the idea for the record in February of that year, while playing in Archie Shepp's band in San Francisco. There he worked out which players and compositions he wanted to use. Alongside him we hear Giuseppi Logan on flute and bass clarinet, Robin Kenyatta on alto saxophone, two bassists, Lewis Worrell and Charlie Haden, and drummer Beaver Harris.

The record contains four long pieces of about twelve minutes each. Everywhere is by Bill Harris, Satan's Dance by Logan. AllMusic called the album intriguing, but far from essential. A KPCC reviewer praised Yankee No-How: the cheerful melody gives way to a group improvisation that works as a single whole. Todd Jenkins thought it was clearly the trombonist's show.
werk/roswell-rudd-everywhere.listen: Listen to Yankee No-How and notice how the cheerful melody gives way to an improvisation in which the whole group plays at once.

werk/roswell-rudd-flexible-flyer.text:
Flexible Flyer was recorded in March 1974 at Blue Rock Studios in New York and released in 1975 by Freedom Records. Trombonist Roswell Rudd plays here with singer Sheila Jordan, pianist Hod O'Brien, bassist Arild Andersen and drummer Barry Altschul. The repertoire ranges from Herbie Hancock's Maiden Voyage and a song by Michel Legrand to original work and pieces by O'Brien.

A JazzTimes reviewer called the record a pearl going against the current. While other musicians in those years were taking new paths, Rudd moved away from the free jazz of the sixties for which he had become known. He sought a mix of cheerful swing and reflective lyricism. The rhythm section is described as tight yet adventurous. Giddins found the use of the voice on the standards less successful.
werk/roswell-rudd-flexible-flyer.listen: Listen to Moselle Variations, the longest track, and hear how the piece consists of three parts. What role does the trombone play in each part?

werk/rowwen-heze-bestel-mar.text: Rowwen Hèze came from the small Limburg village of America and sang in the dialect of North Limburg. Their music was a mixture of rock, polka, Tex-Mex and Irish folk, with an accordion. Bestel mar, from 1991, became a singalong at every party and festival in the south of the Netherlands. Like Normaal, they showed that music from the region could attract a large audience, far beyond their own area.
werk/rowwen-heze-bestel-mar.listen: Bestel mar is a cheerful drinking song. Hear the accordion and the Limburg dialect.

werk/roxette-joyride.text:
Joyride is the third studio album by the Swedish pop duo Roxette. It was released on 25 March 1991, as the follow-up to Look Sharp! and to the single It Must Have Been Love from the film Pretty Woman. Recording took eleven months. Per Gessle began with demos in Halmstad in February 1990, after which Marie Fredriksson joined in and recording continued in Stockholm with producer Clarence Öfwerman.

The record company pressed for a move to Los Angeles and for American producers, but the duo chose their own Swedish musicians. Gessle wrote almost thirty songs and wanted the album to sound like a collection of hits. Fredriksson wrote the music for the ballad Watercolors in the Rain. The title song became the first number one in Sweden. The album topped the chart in seven European countries. AllMusic called it the work of two pop artists at the top of their form.
werk/roxette-joyride.listen: Listen to Watercolors in the Rain and notice how this quiet song, with more folk music in it, differs from the hit singles.

werk/roxette-look-sharp.text:
Two years after their debut, Per Gessle and Marie Fredriksson recorded their second album between March and September 1988, at EMI Studios in Stockholm and Trident II Studios in London. In Sweden the record went straight to number 1. Elsewhere, success was at first modest, until an American exchange student from Minneapolis took the album home with him and gave a copy to his local radio station. The Look became popular there, while the duo still had no record deal in the United States. The song reached number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and in 25 countries.

This made Look Sharp! the international breakthrough. Listen to Your Heart also reached the top of the American chart, Dangerous reached 2 and Dressed for Success 14. Critics were divided: they praised the singles, but found the other songs lighter and less strong.
werk/roxette-look-sharp.listen: Listen to The Look and notice how catchy the chorus is, the song with which the duo broke through in America.

werk/roxette-pearls-of-passion.text:
In the early eighties Per Gessle had three number 1 albums with his band Gyllene Tider, but after its break-up in 1984 his solo records flopped. Marie Fredriksson was successful on the same label, EMI Sweden. On the advice of the label's director, Gessle translated the song Svarta glas into English and recorded it as a duet with Fredriksson: Neverending Love. It became Roxette's first single and reached number three in Sweden. The rest of the album was recorded in the summer of 1986.

Pearls of Passion was released on 31 October 1986 in Scandinavia and Canada. In Sweden it was an immediate success: number two on the album chart. Elsewhere the album did not enter the charts. Goodbye to You and Soul Deep reached the Swedish top twenty. AllMusic was critical and found a lot of average dance music, but called Soul Deep, Neverending Love and Secrets That She Keeps strong.
werk/roxette-pearls-of-passion.listen: Listen to Neverending Love and notice how the voices of Marie Fredriksson and Per Gessle together carry the duet.

werk/roxette-the-look.text: On 8 April 1989 The Look by the Swedish duo Roxette was number one in America. That was thanks to an exchange student from Minnesota, who took the CD with him from Sweden and handed it in at the radio station KDWB in Minneapolis. The station played the song, and other stations followed. After ABBA, Roxette proved once again that Sweden could make English-language worldwide hits. Songwriter Per Gessle wrote it.
werk/roxette-the-look.listen: Hear the raw guitar riff and the short, loose phrases. The lyrics sometimes sound like nonsense, but you keep singing them.

werk/roxette-tourism.text:
Tourism was released on 28 August 1992 as Roxette's fourth studio album. It is often mistaken for a live album, but the group itself called it a tour record: the material was recorded in all kinds of places during the Join the Joyride! Tour. It contains three concert recordings, and Never Is a Long Time was recorded in an empty nightclub in São Paulo. Two songs were created in room 603 of the Alvear Palace Hotel in Buenos Aires.

The majority was made in Stockholm, and a new version of It Must Have Been Love, with pedal steel by Greg Leisz, at Ocean Way in Los Angeles. In the United States sales lagged far behind those of Joyride and reviews were mixed; in Europe it did become a success. AllMusic called it the best introduction to the group, with almost no filler.
werk/roxette-tourism.listen: Listen to Never Is a Long Time, recorded live in an empty nightclub, and notice whether you can hear the space around the musicians.

werk/roxy-music-country-life.text:
Country Life is Roxy Music's fourth album and was released on 15 November 1974. Bryan Ferry took the title from a British magazine about country living. With this album the band entered the American top forty for the first time. The single All I Want Is You reached number twelve in Britain.

Opener The Thrill of It All is a fast rocker. Eddie Jobson's violin dominates Out of the Blue, which became a favourite on stage. In Bitter-Sweet a German oompah can be heard, Triptych has an Elizabethan feel and If It Takes All Night leans on boogie and blues. Casanova was acclaimed as a more cynical and harder song. The cover with two scantily clad women was censored in, among other places, the United States and Spain. Many critics see this as one of the group's most refined and consistent records.
werk/roxy-music-country-life.listen: In Out of the Blue, listen to Eddie Jobson's violin, which dominates the song, and notice how the flanging effect colours the sound.

werk/roxy-music-for-your-pleasure.text:
Bryan Ferry studied under the pop art painter Richard Hamilton, and you can hear it in the way he put his second album together: as a collage of ideas that clash or else blend. He wrote most of it in two weeks at the beginning of 1973. The band recorded it in February at AIR Studios in London and produced it themselves, with help from Chris Thomas. It was the last album with synthesizer player Brian Eno.

The production is more elaborate than on the debut. In Every Dream Home a Heartache, a sinister ode to an inflatable doll, fades away and returns with all the instruments in a strong phasing effect. The Bogus Man revolves around a metronome-like rhythm and an atonal saxophone. The album reached number four on the British chart, received good reviews and is regarded as one of the best glam rock albums. The cover with Amanda Lear and a black panther became just as famous.
werk/roxy-music-for-your-pleasure.listen: In In Every Dream Home a Heartache, listen to the ending, where the song fades away and then returns with a strong phasing effect on all the instruments.

werk/roxy-music-manifesto.text:
After almost four years without a studio record, Roxy Music returned in March 1979 with Manifesto, the first recording since Siren in 1975. Bryan Ferry designed the cover together with fashion designer Antony Price: a group of shop-window mannequins, with a typeface and a title that go back to the first issue of Wyndham Lewis's magazine Blast. On the LP the first side was called East Side and the second West Side.

The sound moves towards the American radio of the time. Trash was the first single. Dance Away took on a disco colouring and reached number two in England, one of the group's biggest hits. Angel Eyes was re-recorded, more electronic than the power-pop version on the LP. Critics were positive, although they found it less strong than earlier work. Robert Christgau called it not the most innovative, but the most listenable, with a relaxed, funky groove on the West Side.
werk/roxy-music-manifesto.listen: Listen to Dance Away and notice how disco comes through in the relaxed, funky rhythm of this song.

werk/roxy-music-siren.text:
Siren is Roxy Music's fifth studio album, released on 24 October 1975 by Island Records, and in the United States by Atco. Chris Thomas produced it. The sound is more direct and poppier than before: according to the critic Simon Frith, less electronic clutter and more solo playing. Eddie Jobson played violin and synthesizers, John Gustafson bass. The cover shows the model Jerry Hall on the rocks at South Stack on Anglesey. Bryan Ferry thought of the location after a TV documentary.

Love Is the Drug became the biggest hit, number two in the United Kingdom and number thirty in the US, the band's highest position there. Both Ends Burning reached number 25 in the United Kingdom. In 2003 Rolling Stone placed Siren at number 371 on its list of the five hundred greatest albums. Stephen Thomas Erlewine called the record a classic, while Simon Reynolds found it conventional and tame.
werk/roxy-music-siren.listen: Listen to Love Is the Drug and notice how the danceable rhythm section carries Bryan Ferry's vocals.

werk/roxy-music-stranded.text:
Stranded was released in 1973 as Roxy Music's third album. It was the first record without synthesizer player Brian Eno, who had been replaced by Eddie Jobson. For the first time Bryan Ferry was not the only writer: Andy Mackay and Phil Manzanera also supplied songs. Chris Thomas produced. The cover shows the model Marilyn Cole, styled as someone stranded in the jungle.

The band sounded somewhat more straightforward, with more piano and heavy guitars. Even so, the music sometimes remained unsettled, AllMusic later wrote. The record topped the British album chart, and Street Life reached number nine on the singles chart. In 1974 Rolling Stone felt that Americans could no longer ignore Roxy Music. Eno himself later called it one of his favourite albums by the group.
werk/roxy-music-stranded.listen: In Street Life, listen to the guitars and keyboards beneath Ferry's vocals, and notice how full and tight the sound is.

werk/roy-ayers-stoned-soul-picnic.text:
Stoned Soul Picnic is the third studio album by the vibraphonist Roy Ayers. It was released in 1968 on Atlantic Records, with Herbie Mann as producer. Alongside Ayers, the players include Charles Tolliver on trumpet and flugelhorn, Hubert Laws on flute, Gary Bartz on alto saxophone and Herbie Hancock on piano. The bass is played by Ron Carter and Miroslav Vitous, and Grady Tate is on drums.

Striking is the choice of songs by others: Stoned Soul Picnic by Laura Nyro, Wave by Antonio Carlos Jobim and For Once in My Life. Charles Tolliver and Edwin Birdsong supplied Lil's Paradise and What the People Say, and Ayers himself wrote A Rose for Cindy. AllMusic felt that the group lets the groove bubble through nicely and called the record one of his better jazz-oriented works.
werk/roy-ayers-stoned-soul-picnic.listen: Listen to Wave and notice how the vibraphone carries Jobim's melody and how the band keeps a quiet groove beneath it.

werk/roy-ayers-virgo-vibes.text:
Virgo Vibes, from 1967, is the second album under his own name by the vibraphonist Roy Ayers and was released on Atlantic Records. The record was made in two sessions: on 18 January 1967 at Gold Star Studios in Los Angeles and on 6 March 1967 in New York. As a result two different groups play on it. Trumpeter Charles Tolliver can be heard on both sessions. The tenor saxophone is played by Joe Henderson in New York and by Harold Land in Los Angeles. In The Ringer, Herbie Hancock plays piano, under the pseudonym Ronnie Clark.

The title piece Virgo Vibes lasts almost thirteen minutes and is the longest track. AllMusic called the record one of Ayers's best, made long before he turned to disco and pop, when he was still a promising jazz vibraphonist.
werk/roy-ayers-virgo-vibes.listen: Listen to Virgo Vibes and notice how the longest track on the record gives room to the vibraphone and to the soloists.

werk/roy-eldridge-happy-time.text:
Happy Time is a 1975 studio album by the American jazz trumpeter Roy Eldridge. Norman Granz produced it, and it was released on Pablo Records. He plays trumpet and sings, accompanied by pianist Oscar Peterson, guitarist Joe Pass, bassist Ray Brown and drummer Eddie Locke.

The repertoire consists of ten well-known standards, including Willow Weep for Me, Makin' Whoopee, All of Me, On the Sunny Side of the Street and I Can't Get Started. There is also a blues number by T-Bone Walker, Stormy Monday. The album closes with Let Me Off Uptown, the shortest track on the record. Benny Green wrote the sleeve notes.
werk/roy-eldridge-happy-time.listen: Listen to Willow Weep For Me and notice how the trumpet lays down the melody calmly, while piano, guitar and bass keep playing softly beneath it.

werk/roy-hargrove-diamond-in-the-rough.text:
Diamond in the Rough is trumpeter Roy Hargrove's first album as a bandleader. It was recorded in December 1989 and released in April 1990 on Novus/RCA. Hargrove surrounded himself with trusted musicians: the saxophonists Antonio Hart and Ralph Moore, the pianists Geoffrey Keezer and John Hicks, the bassists Charles Fambrough and Scott Colley and the drummers Al Foster and Ralph Peterson Jr. Larry Clothier produced.

The programme consists of jazz classics, original compositions by Hargrove and Keezer and a ballad associated with Bing Crosby, Easy to Remember. Scott Yanow of AllMusic heard Freddie Hubbard at times in the hard bop, but already a fairly individual sound, with restrained playing on the ballad and strong bop solos elsewhere. His only objection was that the performances and solos were often rather short. Gary Giddins thought the album perhaps a little over-produced, but saw in Hargrove's playing a warm tone, sensible dynamics and surprising calm.
werk/roy-hargrove-diamond-in-the-rough.listen: Listen to Easy to Remember and notice the warm tone of the trumpet and how calmly he lets a melody sing out.

werk/roy-hargrove-public-eye.text:
Public Eye is trumpeter Roy Hargrove's second album. It was recorded in October 1990 and released in March 1991 on Novus/RCA. The band features saxophonist Antonio Hart, pianist Stephen Scott, bassist Christian McBride and drummer Billy Higgins. Larry Clothier was the producer.

The record mixes well-known pieces such as September in the Rain and What's New and a very fast version of Crazeology with strong original songs such as Public Eye and Lada. Scott Yanow heard Hargrove playing in a style not far removed from that of Lee Morgan, but with a soulful sound of his own. The Rolling Stone Album Guide praised the interplay of Hargrove and Hart, of the kind you usually expect from experienced musicians. The Chicago Tribune still missed individuality, while Spin felt that the album shows Hargrove's growth as a bandleader and puts the twenty-two-year-old Hart in the spotlight.
werk/roy-hargrove-public-eye.listen: Listen to Little Bennie (Crazeology) and notice the high tempo and how trumpet and alto saxophone answer each other.

werk/roy-hargrove-the-vibe.text:
The Vibe is trumpeter Roy Hargrove's third studio album and was released on 8 April 1992 on Novus/RCA. He played in a quintet with alto saxophonist Antonio Hart, pianist Marc Cary, bassist Rodney Whitaker and drummer Gregory Hutchinson. Guests also took part, including Branford Marsalis, David Fathead Newman and Cap'n Jack McDuff on Hammond organ.

Hargrove was only 22 at the time. Critics already saw in him one of the better trumpeters in hard bop. The AllMusic reviewer called the record a fine example of his rapidly emerging style. Others heard mainly jazz nostalgia for the sixties, and felt that he was still at the beginning of a potentially brilliant career. Of Where Were You?, one journalist wrote that these were ballads in which he felt at home.
werk/roy-hargrove-the-vibe.listen: Listen to Where Were You? and notice how the trumpet lets a ballad breathe: where does he take his time?

werk/roy-orbison-at-the-rock-house.text:
At the Rock House is Roy Orbison's first album on the label Sun Records and was released in 1961 in mono. By then he had already moved to Monument. Sun owner Sam Phillips had recordings from 1956 to 1958 lying around and seized on the singer's national success, with three big hits in 1960 and 1961, to release them. He wrote most of the songs himself, but the credits went to Phillips. They are in Sun's traditional rockabilly style. Apart from Devil Doll, all the tracks were given additional vocals or instruments afterwards.

Rock House is credited to Orbison and Jenkins. Bruce Eder of AllMusic called the album exciting, but understood why it did not break through at the time: songs like You're Gonna Cry and Problem Child were too intense and too ambitious for the rock and roll audience, with many changes and extended lyrics.
werk/roy-orbison-at-the-rock-house.listen: Listen to You're Gonna Cry and notice the many changes within the song, which make it sound more ambitious than ordinary rock and roll.

werk/roy-orbison-in-dreams.text:
In Dreams is Roy Orbison's fourth studio album. Monument Records released it in July 1963, in stereo and in mono. It was recorded at RCA Studio B in Nashville, Tennessee. The record is named after the single In Dreams, which entered the Billboard Hot 100 in February 1963 and reached number seven there.

Alongside original work there are covers, such as All I Have to Do Is Dream, Dream and My Prayer. Orbison wrote or co-wrote four of the songs. Blue Bayou was a second single and reached number three in the United Kingdom. Thom Jurek of AllMusic heard emotion and deep atmosphere in the music, and found the choice of songs excellent. In the United Kingdom the album spent 58 weeks on the chart and reached number six. In 2004 Rolling Stone placed the title song at number 319 on its list of the 500 greatest songs.
werk/roy-orbison-in-dreams.listen: In In Dreams, listen to the emotion and the atmosphere that Orbison builds with his voice, and notice how the accompaniment stays with him.

werk/roy-orbison-lonely-and-blue.text:
Lonely and Blue is Roy Orbison's debut album and was released in January 1961 on Monument Records, in stereo and mono. After two years at Sun Records he signed with RCA in 1958, but left after two singles. In early 1959 his manager Wesley Rose asked Fred Foster of Monument whether he was interested. He was. The album was recorded at RCA Studio B, with two- and three-track recorders.

The album contains Only the Lonely, Blue Angel and I'm Hurtin', which were already known as singles. There are also covers of, among others, Don Gibson, the Everly Brothers and Johnnie Ray. Come Back to Me (My Love) has almost the same intro as Only the Lonely, because that is where the vocal figure of Only the Lonely comes from. AllMusic praised the powerful vocals and the saxophone solo by Boots Randolph in I'll Say It's My Fault. In Britain the album entered the chart in 1963.
werk/roy-orbison-lonely-and-blue.listen: Listen to Come Back to Me (My Love) and notice the intro, which sounds almost the same as that of Only the Lonely.

werk/run-dmc-back-from-hell.text:
Back from Hell was released on 16 October 1990 on Profile Records and is Run-D.M.C.'s fifth album. The group produced it themselves, in a difficult time. Jam Master Jay had tax debts, Run was struggling with severe depression and DMC drank heavily to keep his stage fright in check. Their popularity had fallen considerably, especially in comparison with West Coast rappers.

The album took on a rawer, more street-oriented tone, with more coarse language and fewer rock influences. Faces and Pause brought a new style to the group, new jack swing. On Don't Stop, Aaron Hall sings, and Jam Master Jay raps himself for the first time. The criticism was mixed: Rolling Stone did not find the lyrics convincing, but praised Jay's music, which layers samples on samples without overdoing it.
werk/run-dmc-back-from-hell.listen: Listen to Pause and notice the new sound of new jack swing, with a tight beat. Can you hear Jam Master Jay rapping himself?

werk/rush-2112.text:
After the disappointing sales of Fly by Night and Caress of Steel, Rush was in a bad way in 1976. The money had run out, the tour was called the Down the Tubes Tour by the band itself, and Mercury considered dropping the group. Manager Ray Danniels managed to secure one more album. The label and the manager wanted more commercial music, but the band kept to its progressive course.

The first side is filled entirely by the twenty-minute title piece, a story set in a distant future. The second side consists of shorter songs that show the group's hard rock roots. The record received favourable reviews, soon sold better than the earlier albums and became the first big success. Afterwards the band took full creative control into its own hands.
werk/rush-2112.listen: Listen to 2112: Overture and notice how the twenty-minute title piece opens, as a run-up to a story that fills the whole of the first side.

werk/rush-a-farewell-to-kings.text:
A Farewell to Kings was released on 29 August 1977 and was Rush's fifth studio album. The group had just reached a peak with 2112 and the tour that followed, including their first European shows. For the follow-up they wanted to record outside Toronto for the first time. Producer Terry Brown found Rockfield Studios in Wales, where the record was made in about three weeks.

The group broadened its sound with more synthesizers, and each member played more instruments than before. Neil Peart added tubular bells and chimes to his drum kit, among other things, Geddy Lee used a Minimoog and Alex Lifeson a Moog Taurus bass pedal. The album contains long and short songs. Xanadu lasts eleven minutes, Closer to the Heart less than three, and both became concert favourites. Cygnus X-1 Book I: The Voyage ends with a cliffhanger that is continued on the next album, Hemispheres. The criticism was mostly positive, and the album helped the group further internationally.
werk/rush-a-farewell-to-kings.listen: Listen to Xanadu and notice the first five minutes without vocals: which sounds build an atmosphere here before the rock band comes in?

werk/rush-caress-of-steel.text:
Caress of Steel is Rush's third studio album and was released on 24 September 1975 on Mercury. The band recorded it in July at Toronto Sound Studios, immediately after the tour for Fly by Night. Guitarist Alex Lifeson, bassist Geddy Lee and drummer Neil Peart felt confident and were proud of the result. They built on the long, conceptual songs of the previous record and moved from bluesy hard rock towards prog rock.

The Necromancer lasts twelve minutes and is influenced by Tolkien. The Fountain of Lamneth fills the second side and was the group's first epic prog rock song. Bastille Day and Lakeside Park remained fixtures of the live set. Even so, the album proved to be a low point. The darker sound and the fantasy stories found little audience, sales stayed low and the tour was nicknamed Down the Tubes. Fans have valued the record more in retrospect.
werk/rush-caress-of-steel.listen: Listen to The Fountain of Lamneth and follow how the piece consists of six parts and tells a story about a man in search of the source, with mainly a drum solo in the second part.

werk/rush-fly-by-night.text:
Fly by Night was released on 14 February 1975 and was Rush's second album. It was the first with drummer Neil Peart, who replaced John Rutsey in the summer of 1974, just before the first North American tour. Peart also became the main lyricist, and his imaginative and philosophical themes differed greatly from the simpler hard rock of the debut. Recording took about five days in Toronto, with Terry Brown as co-producer.

Each song shows a different side of the band. Anthem is named after a novel by Ayn Rand. By-Tor and the Snow Dog lasts eight minutes and consists of eight parts. It tells a battle between good and evil and marked an important point in the group's writing. Rivendell is also fantasy, and Fly by Night is about Peart's move from Canada to London. In the United States the album sold modestly; in Canada it reached number 9.
werk/rush-fly-by-night.listen: Listen to By-Tor and the Snow Dog and notice the different parts: how does the music change as the story of the struggle between the two characters unfolds?

werk/rush-rush.text:
Rush is the debut album of the Canadian band, five years after its formation. It was released on 18 March 1974 in Canada on Moon Records, the group's own label, and came out internationally later that year on Mercury. It is the only record with the first drummer John Rutsey. The band did not think the first recordings, in the summer of 1973, sounded good enough. In November they partly re-recorded the album and remixed it entirely with Terry Brown, and three new songs were added. The sound is direct hard rock on the model of Led Zeppelin and Humble Pie.

Working Man did well on a radio station in Cleveland, where listeners phoned to ask where they could buy the record. That led to an international contract. Billboard heard something of Robert Plant in Geddy Lee's singing. Later critics judged it more severely, because Neil Peart was not yet part of it.
werk/rush-rush.listen: Listen to Working Man and notice Geddy Lee's singing, which reminded Billboard of Robert Plant, and the powerful guitar work.

werk/ry-cooder-boomer-s-story.text:
Boomer's Story is the third studio album by the American roots musician Ry Cooder and was released in November 1972. A few guests take part on the record. There are two songs by Sleepy John Estes on the record, Ax Sweet Mama and President Kennedy. Estes sings the lead himself on the second, and his parts were recorded in Collierville, Tennessee.

The piano on Rally 'Round the Flag is played by Randy Newman. The Dark End of the Street, written by Dan Penn and Chips Moman, is best known as a recording by James Carr, but here it sounds like an instrumental in which the guitar carries the melody.
werk/ry-cooder-boomer-s-story.listen: Listen to Dark End of the Street and notice how the guitar takes the place of the singer and carries the melody of the song.

werk/ry-cooder-into-the-purple-valley.text:
Into the Purple Valley is Ry Cooder's second studio album and was released in 1972. The record is rooted almost entirely in older American music. Cooder plays songs by Lead Belly and Woody Guthrie, but also calypso and gospel, such as F.D.R. in Trinidad and Denomination Blues. He plays guitar and mandolin and sings himself. Among the contributors are Van Dyke Parks on keyboards and Jim Keltner on drums.

The album mixes folk, blues and small bands in a warm, loose atmosphere. Teardrops Will Fall was a hit for Dickey Doo & the Don'ts in 1959, but Cooder himself knew the song from Wilson Pickett. Vigilante Man is by Woody Guthrie. Record Collector wrote that the record reached deep into the tradition and dug up forgotten treasures from the American past to reshape them for the post-Woodstock generation. The cover, too, with Cooder and his then wife in a Buick, appears on a Rolling Stone list.
werk/ry-cooder-into-the-purple-valley.listen: Listen to Vigilante Man and notice the guitar and the vocals: what mood does Cooder give this song by Woody Guthrie?

werk/ry-cooder-paradise-and-lunch.text:
Paradise and Lunch was released on 8 June 1974 and was Ry Cooder's fourth album. Russ Titelman and Lenny Waronker produced it at the Warner Brothers studios. The record consists of covers of jazz, blues and roots, both well-known standards and obscure songs. Cooder plays guitar and mandolin and is assisted by, among others, Jim Keltner on drums and Plas Johnson on saxophone.

Striking is Tattler, Cooder's version of a song by the bluesman Washington Phillips, known above all for its guitar playing. Linda Ronstadt and David Soul later recorded it as well. In Jesus on the Mainline and It's All Over Now he draws on gospel and rhythm and blues. The closing track Ditty Wah Ditty is a duet with the jazz pianist Earl Hines. The album reached number 167 on the Billboard 200 and was later reissued, including in a remastered version in 2007.
werk/ry-cooder-paradise-and-lunch.listen: Listen to Ditty Wah Ditty and notice the interplay between Cooder's guitar and Earl Hines's piano: who takes the lead in each section?

werk/ryuichi-sakamoto-esperanto.text:
Esperanto is Ryuichi Sakamoto's fifth solo album and was released in 1985. It was made on commission for a dance of the same name by the choreographer Molissa Fenley, which premiered in New York that year. It is experimental electronic music with layers of sampled voices and looks back to his second solo album B-2 Unit, which was not aimed at pop. Yaz-Kaz and Arto Lindsay took part. The album reached number nine on the Oricon LP chart. It was released on the label School of Midi, Inc. and was not issued in the United States until 2021.

The dance received a mixed review in The New York Times, and according to the critic the music sounded like a radio being switched on and off again and again. The album itself later received better reviews. AllMusic calls it one of the creator's strangest, most uncompromising albums, with an icy soundscape. According to that source, Adelic Penguins comes closest to techno.
werk/ryuichi-sakamoto-esperanto.listen: In Adelic Penguins, listen to the fragments of melody that leap up above a driving bass line.

werk/sam-phillips-martinis-en-bikinis.text:
Martinis & Bikinis is the seventh album by the American singer and songwriter Sam Phillips. It was released on 8 March 1994 and was reissued in 2012. T Bone Burnett produced the record. Drummer Mickey Curry, bassist Jerry Scheff and guitarist David Mansfield are among the regular musicians, and guests include Peter Buck, Marc Ribot, Benmont Tench and Van Dyke Parks.

Colin Moulding is co-producer of the fourth track, for which Parks arranged the strings. The album is dedicated to the actor River Phoenix. Circle of Fire was nominated for Best Female Rock Vocal Performance at the 37th Grammy Awards.
werk/sam-phillips-martinis-en-bikinis.listen: Listen to Baby I Can't Please You, the song with Colin Moulding as co-producer, and notice the strings that Van Dyke Parks arranged.

werk/sam-phillips-the-indescribable-wow.text:
The Indescribable Wow is Sam Phillips's fifth studio album, and her first for Virgin Records. With it she moved from Christian pop to secular alternative rock. She also used a different name: Sam instead of Leslie. T Bone Burnett produced the record. He also played guitar, mandocello and Marxophone, and Van Dyke Parks wrote the arrangements for one song. Harpsichord, harmonium and cello can also be heard, among other instruments.

The single Holding On to the Earth reached number 22 on the Billboard Modern Rock Tracks in early 1989. The record was well received. Rolling Stone called Phillips a great talent with a great deal to offer, and AllMusic found the music timeless.
werk/sam-phillips-the-indescribable-wow.listen: In Holding On to the Earth, listen to the unusual instruments alongside the guitars, and notice how her voice carries the song.

werk/sam-rivers-a-new-conception.text:
A New Conception is the third album by the American saxophonist Sam Rivers. He recorded it in 1966 for Blue Note, with Hal Galper on piano, Herbie Lewis on bass and Steve Ellington on drums. Rivers plays tenor and soprano saxophone and flute.

The album consists of seven jazz standards, such as When I Fall in Love, Detour Ahead and Secret Love. The saxophonist gives these familiar songs a new shape in his own arrangements. AllMusic called the music challenging but accessible, because familiar themes are rearranged in surprising ways. The reviewer praised the skill in the arrangements and felt that Rivers's talent was unjustly underrated.
werk/sam-rivers-a-new-conception.listen: Listen to When I Fall in Love and try to follow the familiar theme as the saxophone plays it slightly differently each time.

werk/sam-rivers-contours.text:
Contours is saxophonist Sam Rivers's second album for Blue Note. He recorded it in 1965, and it was released on the label afterwards. Rivers plays tenor saxophone, soprano saxophone and flute. He works with trumpeter Freddie Hubbard, pianist Herbie Hancock, bassist Ron Carter and drummer Joe Chambers. He wrote all four pieces himself.

According to an AllMusic reviewer, Rivers embraced the avant-garde here, but presented it in a way that would not frighten or confuse lovers of hard bop. The same reviewer called the record rarely less than fascinating and one of the high points of the avant-garde in the mid-sixties. The CD reissue includes a second take of Mellifluous Cacophony as a bonus.
werk/sam-rivers-contours.listen: Listen to Euterpe and notice how the soloists give each other room in a piece that sounds free yet keeps a clear line.

werk/sam-rivers-crystals.text:
Crystals was released in September 1974 on Impulse! in stereo and quadraphonic. Sam Rivers wrote the pieces between 1959 and 1972 and finished them as new elements arose that brought them together conceptually. Earlier, Ornette Coleman with his Free Jazz Double Quartet and John Coltrane with Ascension had already deployed large line-ups, and the Jazz Composers' Orchestra Association had existed for a few years.

Recording took five or six hours. The line-up is sometimes put at fourteen musicians: three trumpets, two trombones, tuba, five reed players, bass and two drummers. Rivers plays saxophone and conducts. After a few years the record could no longer be obtained, and it was released on CD in 2002. The critic Thom Jurek heard in it the mature Rivers as composer, improviser and thinker.
werk/sam-rivers-crystals.listen: Listen to Exultation and notice how the large ensemble sounds as a whole, while the individual horns remain audible.

werk/sam-rivers-fuchsia-swing-song.text:
Fuchsia Swing Song is the debut album of the American saxophonist Sam Rivers. He recorded it in 1964 for Blue Note, with Jaki Byard on piano, Ron Carter on bass and Tony Williams on drums. All six compositions are by the leader himself.

At that moment Rivers was under the influence of John Coltrane and Ornette Coleman, but had not yet let go of the blues. As a result the record sounds like the work of a musician who is confident and at the same time in motion. Downstairs Blues Upstairs shows that link with the blues in its very title. According to the AllMusic reviewer, Rivers never played like this again, and he called it a highly recommended record. The album later appeared on CD, in 2003 with four alternate takes added.
werk/sam-rivers-fuchsia-swing-song.listen: Listen to Downstairs Blues Upstairs and notice how the tenor saxophone both sustains and breaks open the blues.

werk/santana-abraxas.text:
Abraxas is Santana's second studio album and was released on 23 September 1970 on Columbia Records. It became the band's first album to top the American Billboard 200. The title comes from the book Demian by Hermann Hesse, from which a quotation appears on the back of the sleeve. The cover itself shows the painting Annunciation by Mati Klarwein, which Carlos Santana saw in a magazine.

The band plays a mixture of rock and Latin rhythms. Black Magic Woman is a version of a song by Fleetwood Mac, to which Gypsy Queen by Gábor Szabó has been added. Oye Como Va was a hit for Tito Puente in the early sixties and was played live because the audience could dance to it so well. Samba Pa Ti is an instrumental. In 2015 the Library of Congress added the album to the National Recording Registry.
werk/santana-abraxas.listen: Listen to Black Magic Woman / Gypsy Queen and notice how the song changes mood when the second part begins.

werk/santana-borboletta.text:
Borboletta is Santana's sixth studio album and belongs to the band's jazz-funk fusion, together with Caravanserai and Welcome. The guitarist leaves plenty of room for percussion, saxophone and keyboards, which set the mood, as in Spring Manifestations. He himself plays long solos, as in Promise of a Fisherman, and in Give and Take you hear a funky, guitar-driven song with vocals.

The line-up changed. David Brown returned as bassist to replace Doug Rauch, on some tracks Stanley Clarke plays bass, and Leon Patillo joined as singer and keyboardist. After recording finished, drummer Michael Shrieve left and was succeeded by Leon Ndugu Chancler, who had already played on parts of the album.
werk/santana-borboletta.listen: Listen to Give and Take and notice how the guitar carries the song alongside the vocals.

werk/santana-caravanserai.text:
Caravanserai is Santana's fourth studio album, released on 11 October 1972 by Columbia. It came out of a transitional period: it was the last record with several early members, and the music moved towards instrumental, progressive jazz fusion. It was recorded at Columbia Studios in San Francisco, in March, April and May 1972, produced by the guitarist himself and drummer Michael Shrieve.

The album sold less than the earlier hit records and reached number eight on the Billboard chart, but later went platinum. According to Shrieve, Clive Davis said the band was committing career suicide. Critics saw it as an artistic success. Ralph Gleason wrote in Rolling Stone that it spoke to the universality of man.
werk/santana-caravanserai.listen: In Eternal Caravan of Reincarnation, listen to the saxophone intro with which the record opens and hear how calmly and instrumentally Santana begins here.

werk/santana-welcome.text:
Welcome is Santana's fifth studio album, released in 1973. It follows the jazz fusion of Caravanserai, but with a different line-up: Gregg Rolie and Neal Schon left to start Journey and were replaced by Tom Coster, Richard Kermode and Leon Thomas. Guests include John McLaughlin, Alice Coltrane on piano in Going Home and Flora Purim on vocals.

The album is far more experimental than the first four and produced no hit single. Robert Palmer wrote in Rolling Stone that the rhythm section sounds relaxed and at its best. Thom Jurek of AllMusic called it a jazz record with rock elements, ahead of its time and one of the band's most enduring recordings.
werk/santana-welcome.listen: In Yours Is the Light, listen to Flora Purim's singing.

werk/sarah-mclachlan-fumbling-towards-ec.text:
Fumbling Towards Ecstasy was released on 22 October 1993 and is Sarah McLachlan's third album. Producer Pierre Marchand made it in Montreal. McLachlan wrote most of it in a small house close to his studio. In Canada, where she was already known, it was an immediate hit. Elsewhere it grew slowly: in the United States it stayed in the middle of the charts for almost two years.

The album sounds atmospheric and restrained, with soft arrangements and raw, honest lyrics. Critics praised her voice and the depth of the songs. According to an AllMusic reviewer, the record combines Marchand's atmospheric production with her strongest songwriting to date. Rolling Stone wrote that she truly came into her own as an artist here.
werk/sarah-mclachlan-fumbling-towards-ec.listen: Listen to Possession and notice her voice and the atmosphere that the production builds around it.
